thread.title: Regulation Is the Risk as Facebook, Twitter, Head to Congress

author: Jon Swartz
title: Regulation Is the Risk as Facebook, Twitter, Head to Congress
text:
Sheryl Sandberg, chief operating officer of Facebook and Jack Dorsey, CEO of Twitter. Photo: Joel Arbaje; Source Photos Getty Images By Jon Swartz Aug. 31, 2018 9:33 a.m. ET Silicon Valley and the Beltway have often been accused of living in bubbles, unfamiliar with and wary of others—especially each other. The enmity stretches back decades to unsuccessful attempts by the federal government to bust up IBM and Microsoft, and recent rumbles to rein in social media companies .
The great disconnect between the two, increasingly exacerbated by the growing political and cultural clout of the tech economy, will be on show next week when leaders from Facebook (ticker: FB) and Twitter (TWTR) testify before the Senate Intelligence Committee on their efforts to police political content. Facebook Chief Operating Officer Sheryl Sandberg and Twitter Chief Executive Jack Dorsey are scheduled to appear on Sept. 5; Alphabet (GOOGL) has been invited, but won’t commit to making CEO Larry Page available. A separate House Energy and Commerce hearing focused on Twitter is also scheduled.
Things were already tense with the threat of regulation looming over social media before President Trump this week claimed Google search results were “rigged” to show mostly “bad” stories about him and conservatives. He later included Facebook and Twitter in his wrath when he warned they were “treading on very, very troubled territory and they have to be careful.”
The political heat on Facebook and Twitter has reached white-hot intensity over their susceptibility to foreign interests digitally manipulating their vast platforms to influence the 2016 presidential election, political contests in other countries, and the forthcoming midterms. It didn’t help matters, either, when The Wall Street Journal reported last week that Altaba ’s (AABA) Yahoo scans customers’ email for data to sell to advertisers.
“We believe the best way to tackle interference is to work with other companies, government, and independent experts,” Facebook spokesman Andy Stone tells Barron’s . “We look forward to sharing with the Senate Intelligence Committee the work we’re doing to prevent bad actors from abusing our service.”
Twitter declined to comment, but a person familiar with its strategy said it will demonstrate to legislators measures it’s taken to “protect the integrity and health” of public discussion on its system ahead of the midterms. Dorsey, who we profiled in a recent cover story , has made it his personal mission to rid the platform of suspicious activity.
Google, which has been fined billions by the European Commission for anticompetitive business practices, has deftly avoided being pulled into the U.S. debate. It did not respond to an email message seeking comment.
Sound familiar?
Next week’s hearings, nearly a year after Senate Democrats and Republicans excoriated the same three companies for failing to thwart what they called Kremlin-aligned interests’ attempts to influence the 2016 election, highlights the Valley’s precarious standing in the nation’s capital. Members of both parties have vowed to punish tech’s biggest names if it doesn’t stop, which could have major ramifications for investors.
Trump, whose fondness for Twitter and Facebook has bordered on the obsessive, has used both media to effectively advance his agenda, bludgeon critics, and generally communicate. It is unlikely much will come of his complaints, but regulation remains a real possibility.
One bill, co-authored by Sens. Mark Warner (D., Va.) and Amy Klobuchar (D., Minn.) would apply the same rules to political ads on the web as those for TV, radio, and satellite.
It all seems inevitable because, try as they might, tech companies find themselves in a quandary.
When a chastened Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg repeatedly apologized to members of Congress this spring about data security and privacy shortcomings at the social-networking giant, he vowed to do better. The company, as well as Twitter, have thrown resources into clamping down on suspicious accounts and misinformation campaigns, with some recent results. In late July, Facebook said it disabled 32 pages and profiles that some Congressional members tied to Russia.
But in their clean-up efforts, tech giants are facing accusations of censorship. House Majority Leader Kevin McCarthy (R., Calif.) has accused Twitter of “shadow banning” the views of conservative voices following the ouster of right-wing conspiracy theorist Alex Jones from Facebook, Apple (AAPL), Spotify Technology (SPOT), and Alphabet’s YouTube. Twitter booted Jones for a week.
In politics, as in tech, it usually comes down to the last word. In this case, D.C. ultimately has the upper hand and home-court advantage.
